title: The corpus_* tool surface, and a routing rule that says when to reach for it
background: After US-43.3 the tier is complete and unreachable from an agent, which is the state a capability dies in. This repo has a measured case: knowledge_context was allowlisted everywhere, documented, and got ONE call in roughly 2100 searches. The audit that found it also found that availability is not what drives tool choice — agents run the verb the protocol prescribes, so the protocol has to prescribe it. A new search verb with no line in a routing table saying which question shape it answers is a tool that exists and is never called. This story therefore has two halves of comparable weight: the mcp-server tool definitions, and the routing prose that makes an agent reach for corpus_search instead of knowledge_search at the right moment.

story.as_a: an agent that has just been asked a question about an authoritative reference document
story.i_want_to: have a corpus_search tool available AND a routing rule that tells me this is the question it answers
story.so_that: I quote the actual page instead of searching the wiki for a distillation of it, or concluding nothing exists

rationale: The routing paragraph is not documentation polish, it is the mechanism. The KB's own measurement is that a surfaced-but-unrouted capability converges on zero use regardless of how good it is. Writing the tool without the routing rule would ship the same outcome knowledge_context got, and the epic would read as complete while changing nothing about what agents actually do.

acceptance_criteria.description: mcp-server declares corpus_create, corpus_index, corpus_search, corpus_list, corpus_status and corpus_delete as statically-declared typed tools, following the existing definition-plus-dispatch-case pattern in mcp-server/index.js, with path-building logic placed in lib/http-helpers.js so it is importable and unit-testable rather than embedded in the stdio entry point.

Each tool description states the TRADE-OFF a caller needs before calling, not just the parameters: corpus_search returns pointers and snippets rather than bodies and the agent must open the file; a mode B corpus is semantic-only because there is no text to index; corpus_delete is irreversible and user-role. These are stated in the description because that is what a model reads at selection time — a caller should never discover a mode restriction from an error.

mcp-server/README.md — the single source of truth for the tool list — carries the corpus_* family, and mcp-server/CHANGELOG.md records the addition. No count of tools is written anywhere (the doc-hygiene rule: counts are wrong by the next merge).

The loopctl CLAUDE.md Knowledge Wiki section gains a paragraph and a routing-table row distinguishing the tier from the three existing information surfaces, keyed on the SHAPE of the question: quote me the exact text of an authoritative document goes to corpus_search; what did we learn about X goes to knowledge_search; a live structured business row goes to retrieve_*; a fact only I need goes to memory_remember. The row states what corpus_search returns (a pointer plus a snippet, not a body) so the caller knows the next step is to open the file.

The routing rule names the failure it prevents in one clause — searching the wiki for a distillation of a document whose verbatim text you needed, or reading an empty wiki result as an empty corpus. A rule that only says what to call is weaker than one that says what going wrong looks like.

Role visibility is handled honestly rather than invented. There is NO role filtering in the MCP server's ListTools — it returns the static TOOLS array unconditionally plus the tenant's generated cr_* tools — and there is no server-side allowlist of MCP tool NAMES anywhere; role is enforced only by RequireRole on the HTTP endpoint, with the client choosing which env key to send. So corpus_delete is listed like every other tool and its description states that it is user-role and irreversible, and the story does NOT build an allowlist layer. Making the tools visible to SUBAGENTS is a separate matter: each agent definition in claude-config carries an explicit tools: frontmatter list, so a mcp__loopctl__corpus_* tool is invisible to every one of them until added there. That is a cross-repo change and is named in this story's closing report as unmade, not silently skipped.

mcp-server tests cover the new tools in the style of the existing knowledge_tools.test.js: the argument forwarding, the path building for each tool, and at least one test asserting that a mode B search forwards a vector rather than a query string.

An end-to-end test indexes a small corpus through the MCP tool surface and searches it, asserting the returned pointer identifies a chunk that was actually indexed. This is the only test in the epic that exercises the whole path an agent uses, and it is what proves the tier is reachable rather than merely present.

mcp-server/package.json is version-bumped in the SAME PR as the index.js, lib/ and README changes. The mcp-server-ci.yml version-bump job fails a PR that touches the published files without one, with the message that nothing publishes to npm without a version bump so agents keep the OLD tool descriptions while the server serves the new payload — a failure mode that shipped six times before the guard existed. The required branch-protection context is the MCP Server Gate job, not the Node unit tests job.

test_cases.name: each corpus tool builds the right path
preconditions: the exported path builders in lib/http-helpers.js
expected_results: unset optional params are omitted from the query string

test_cases.name: mode B search forwards a vector
preconditions: a corpus_search call carrying a query vector
expected_results: no query string field is synthesised

test_cases.name: end-to-end index and search through the tool surface
preconditions: a running server and a small document set
steps: corpus_search for a phrase in one of them
expected_results: the top result names the source_ref and locator of the chunk that contains it

test_cases.name: the routing table names the corpus tier
steps: read the Knowledge Wiki routing section
expected_results: a row keys the quote-the-document question shape to corpus_search
it states that a pointer, not a body, comes back
it names the failure the rule prevents

test_cases.name: no tool count is written into any doc
preconditions: the docs changed by this story
steps: grep for a numeric tool count
expected_results: the README remains the list itself rather than a tally

technical_notes: The routing paragraph belongs in loopctl's CLAUDE.md, which every session and subagent on this repo is guaranteed to read. The claude-config half — a line in the user-level routing guidance so sessions in OTHER repos know the tier exists — is a cross-repo change and is NOT this story. Say so explicitly in the story's closing report rather than leaving it implied, the way US-42.2's AC-42.2.7 did.

Write the tool descriptions for a model choosing between verbs, not for a human reading a manual. The distinguishing sentence is the first one: what question does this answer that knowledge_search does not. Everything after that is parameters.

Do not add the corpus tools to any auto-injected recall or hint block. The tier's discoverability comes from the routing rule, not from injecting rows into every prompt — the injected channel already measures at 5-13% follow-through and adding a second stream of unopened rows would make that worse, not better.

AC-43.4.6 needs the actual mechanism checked at implementation time rather than assumed: confirm whether ListTools filtering is server-side by role, client-side, or absent, and implement visibility in whichever layer actually decides it. If no such mechanism exists, say so in the report and leave corpus_delete visible with its role stated in the description — inventing an allowlist layer is out of scope for this story.
The end-to-end test in AC-43.4.8 is the acceptance criterion the whole epic is judged against. Everything before it can pass with a tier no agent can reach.

Put anything with real logic — query-string building, argument coercion, batch shaping — into mcp-server/lib/ rather than index.js. index.js is a stdio entry point with top-level await, so importing it boots the server and tests cannot reach its handlers; the existing suite RE-IMPLEMENTS handler bodies inside the test file to work around that, which means those tests can pass against a mirror while the shipped code regresses. Code in lib/ is imported and exercised for real.
AC-43.4.9's version bump is easy to forget precisely because it is not part of the feature. Bump it in the same commit that adds the tools, not as a follow-up.
